newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels free 225 hostages, keep about 140.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels free 225 hostages, keep about 140.

text.p: Marxist rebels freed the majority of their hostages from the besieged Japanese embassy residence in Peru on Sunday night but said they were holding onto their government captives as bargaining chips.
At the start of the sixth day of the siege, the guerrillas freed 225 non-government hostages as a Christmas gesture of good faith.

Red Cross mediator Michel Minnig, whose men checked off the freed captives' names from a list, confirmed to reporters outside the residence that 225 were liberated on Sunday night and said just over 140 remained inside.

In a message read before the release began, the guerrillas insisted on their demands for the release of fellow Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) comrades from jail before letting other hostages go.
Looking tired but happy, the freed captives started filing out of the grand front entrance of the embassy just before 10 p.m. local time (0300 GMT Monday) under the gaze of Red Cross officials.
Waiting reporters clapped and cheered as the freed hostages walked unaided out of the embassy compound into the street to board waiting buses.
Those released included diplomats from Britain, Spain, Panama, Honduras, Venezuela, Bolivia, Germany, the European Union, the United Nations and at least four U.S. Embassy staff members.

The hostages appeared to be in good health but were not allowed to stop and talk to reporters before the buses drove them off to a Lima police hospital, where they were greeted by President Alberto Fujimori. Fujimori stayed briefly at the hospital and left without speaking to reporters.

The MRTA guerrillas warned the government in their statement that they would not release Peruvian officials held in the besieged residence unless Fujimori agreed to set free more than 400 jailed MRTA members -- something the government has rejected.
"We clarify and insist that the liberation of the authorities who are today prisoner will only be possible if the government sets free (our) comrades," the MRTA statement said.

It was read to waiting reporters by former labour minister Sandro Fuentes, who was released from the building first to make the statement along with the Panamanian ambassador, the Spanish charge d'affaires and a U.N. official.
"We are proceeding to free people who are not connected to the policy of the regime directly or indirectly as a Christmas gesture," the rebel statement said.
But it also warned the government that "if Mr. Fujimori decides a military solution he will always find a Tupac Amaru (guerrilla)."
The sudden and dramatic mass release came as a surprise because there was no sign of any progress in negotiations.

Conditions inside the grand embassy residence were deteriorating, raising fears of health problems among the hostages. The government cut off running water, electricity and phone service early in the siege.
Just after the siege began its sixth day, several buses drove up outside the residence.
Top government negotiator Domingo Palermo made his first appearance at the scene and Minnig stood by.

After almost an hour of tension and conflicting rumours, the hostages began filing out of the entrance, most still wearing what they had worn for the reception last Tuesday at which they were captured.
Peruvian media reported the release with joy, mingled with regret that no end to the crisis was in sight.
